a1-greetings.title: Greetings: Marhaba and Kifak
a1-greetings.explanation: "مرحبا" (marhaba) is the everyday hello you'll hear everywhere in Syria — shops, taxis, cafés. "كيفك؟" (kifak, to a man) / "كيفك؟" (kifik, to a woman) asks "how are you?" — instantly recognizable as Levantine rather than textbook Arabic. The typical answer is "الحمدلله منيح" (alhamdulillah, mnih — "thank God, good"), with منيح becoming منيحة (mniha) when a woman is speaking about herself.
a1-greetings.fact: "صباح الخير" (sabah el-kheir, good morning) gets answered not by repeating it, but with "صباح النور" (sabah en-noor, literally "morning of light") — like many Arabic greeting pairs, the reply uses a different word entirely rather than echoing the greeting back.

a1-biddi.title: I Want: Biddi
a1-biddi.explanation: "بدي" (biddi) is the everyday way to say "I want" in Syrian Arabic — one of the most common words you'll hear. Just follow it with what you want: "بدي قهوة" (biddi ahwe, "I want coffee").
a1-biddi.fact: بدي is actually بدّ (badd-, "want/need") fused with the possessive ending "-i" (my), so it literally means something like "my wanting" — the same possessive-suffix logic that gives Arabic its other person forms of this word, though this course only teaches the widely-used 1st-person بدي form for now.

dialogue.en: I want coffee today, thank you very much

a1-present-shaf.title: Present Tense: I See, You See...
a1-present-shaf.pattern: ب- / بت- / بتي- / بي- / بت- / من- / بتو- / بي-و
a1-present-shaf.explanation: Syrian present-tense verbs take the ب- (b-) prefix plus a person marker: بشوف (bshuf, "I see"), بتشوف (btshuf, "you-m see"), بتشوفي (btshufi, "you-f see"), بيشوف (byshuf, "he sees"), بتشوف (btshuf, "she sees"), منشوف (mnshuf, "we see"), بتشوفو (btshufu, "you-all see"), بيشوفو (byshufu, "they see").
a1-present-shaf.fact: The 1st person plural "we" prefix (من mn-) looks completely different from the ب- pattern everywhere else — that's not an exception to memorize separately, it's just what happens when ب- fuses with the underlying "n-" marker for "we", a regular sound change across the whole b-prefix system.

dialogue.en: I see a big house today

a1-fi-mafi.title: There Is / There Isn't: Fi and Mafi
a1-fi-mafi.explanation: "فيه" (fi) means "there is/are", and its negative "مافي" (mafi, from ما + فيه) means "there isn't/aren't". This simple pair is so central to everyday Levantine speech that a well-known textbook is literally named "Shou fi ma fi?" ("What's up? / What's there, what's not there?").
a1-fi-mafi.fact: "شو في ما في؟" is itself a common colloquial greeting/small-talk phrase meaning roughly "what's going on?" — literally "what is there, what isn't there" — showing how naturally فيه/مافي gets used beyond its literal grammatical meaning.

dialogue.native: لا، مافي قهوة اليوم، بس في شاي
dialogue.en: No, there's no coffee today, but there's tea

a2-past-katab.title: Past Tense: I Wrote, You Saw...
a2-past-katab.explanation: Levantine past tense uses suffixes on the verb stem: كتبت (katabt, "I wrote"), كتبت (katabt, "you-m wrote"), كتبتِ (katabti, "you-f wrote"), كتب (katab, "he wrote"), كتبت (katbit, "she wrote"), كتبنا (katabna, "we wrote"), كتبتو (katabtoo, "you-all wrote"), كتبو (katabo, "they wrote"). "I" and "you-m" share the exact same form — context tells them apart.
a2-past-katab.fact: The verb شاف (shaf, "to see") follows the same suffix pattern, but as a "hollow" root (ش-و-ف) its long vowel shortens in every person except he/she/they: شفت (shift, "I saw"), شاف (shaf, "he saw"), شافت (shafit, "she saw"), شافو (shafo, "they saw") — the same aa→i shortening pattern found across hollow verbs in Arabic dialects generally.

dialogue.native: شفت بيت كبير وشفت صديق منيح
dialogue.en: I saw a big house and I saw a good friend

a2-past-negation.title: Negating the Past: Ma + Past Verb
a2-past-negation.explanation: To negate a past-tense verb, put ما (ma) right before it: ما شفت (ma shift, "I didn't see"). This is the same ما used for present-tense negation — unlike مش, which is reserved for nominal/participle sentences ("أنا مش تعبان").
a2-past-negation.fact: In fast speech, ما often contracts right onto the verb with barely a pause — ماشفت — but it's still written and thought of as two separate words, ما and شفت, not a single fused word.

dialogue.en: Did you see a friend yesterday?

dialogue.native: لا، ما شفت صديق اليوم، شفت بيت بس
dialogue.en: No, I didn't see a friend today, I only saw a house

a2-days-past.title: Days of the Week with Past Tense
a2-days-past.explanation: Combining a day name with a past-tense verb builds a simple narrative: يوم الجمعة شفت صديق (yom el-jum3a shift sadeeq, "On Friday I saw a friend"). The day name simply comes first, like a time adverb.
a2-days-past.fact: Just like مبارح (yesterday), day names need no extra preposition ("on Friday") — Syrian Arabic places time expressions directly at the start of the sentence.

dialogue.en: On Saturday, what did you see?

dialogue.native: يوم السبت شفت بيت كبير منيح
dialogue.en: On Saturday I saw a big, good house
